section_title: What happens when leaders refuse the message that could give them rest?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, the pride of those overcome by wine. 2 Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty. Like a hailstorm or destructive tempest, like a driving rain or flooding downpour, he will smash that crown to the ground. 3 The majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards will be trampled underfoot. 4 The fading flower of his beautiful splendor, set on the summit above the fertile valley, will be like a ripe fig before the summer harvest: Whoever sees it will take it in his hand and swallow it. 5 On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people, 6 a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate.

7 These also stagger from wine and stumble from strong drink: Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine. They stumble because of strong drink, muddled in their visions and stumbling in their judgments. 8 For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth.

9 Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk? To babies removed from the breast? 10 For they hear: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.” 11 Indeed, with mocking lips and foreign tongues, He will speak to this people 12 to whom He has said: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen. 13 Then the word of the LORD to them will become: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there,” so that they will go stumbling backward and will be injured, ensnared, and captured.

context_lines: The warning begins with Ephraim’s proud crown and fading beauty. A strong attacker is pictured as hail, a destructive storm and flooding rain. What appears glorious will be swallowed as quickly as an early ripe fig.

For the surviving people, the Lord Himself becomes the crown of glory, a source of justice and strength. Yet the next scene exposes priests and prophets staggering under strong drink, failing in the very visions and judgments they are supposed to give.
The questions about teaching infants and the repeated lines about order and line show how badly the message is being received. The Lord had offered rest for the weary, but they would not listen.

Foreign lips and tongues will now become part of how He addresses them. The words they would not receive bring no security to their resistance: the passage ends in stumbling, injury, entrapment and capture.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/28.htm), [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/28.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/28.htm) connect the repeated instruction with people who need to be taught like children but resist learning. They emphasize the contrast between God’s offer of rest and the people’s refusal.

The [Cambridge commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/28.htm) instead reads verses 9–10 as the drunken leaders mocking Isaiah: they resent being addressed like recently weaned children and imitate his repeated instruction. It then reads the foreign speech as the terrible answer to their mockery.
The readings differ over who speaks the repeated words and how they function. Both connect the foreign language with judgment after the people refuse a message they could understand.
god_plan_lines: [First Corinthians 14:20–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/14.htm) directly quotes Isaiah’s warning about foreign tongues and refusal to listen. Paul brings it into his discussion of tongues, prophecy, understanding and the response of unbelievers.

He goes on to describe the danger of an outsider hearing a gathering full of uninterpreted tongues and thinking the believers are out of their minds. By contrast, a message that exposes the heart can lead an unbeliever to fall down and worship God.

The connection keeps the purpose of God’s speech in view. Receiving His message matters more than being impressed by an unusual sound; Paul’s concern is that what happens among believers serves understanding and a right response to God.
